title: Network Policies
summary: By default, Kubernetes allows all pods to communicate with all other pods — a flat network with no isolation. Network Policies are pod-level firewalls that restrict which pods can send or receive traffic and on which ports. Without them, a compromised pod has full lateral movement to every database, API, and service in your cluster.

sections.title: The default open network and why it's dangerous
sections.body:
**Kubernetes default: everything talks to everything.**

```bash
# In a default cluster, any pod can reach any other pod:
# Pod A (namespace: default) → can call Pod B (namespace: database)
# Pod B → can call the Kubernetes API server
# Compromised pod → can port-scan the cluster, reach secrets, databases
```

**Why this matters:**

```
Without Network Policies:
  If an attacker compromises a frontend pod, they can:
    1. Call your database service directly (not just via the app)
    2. Exfiltrate data to external IPs
    3. Call the internal Kubernetes API to read Secrets
    4. Move laterally to backend services not exposed externally

With Network Policies (zero-trust):
  frontend pod → can only reach backend pod on port 8080
  backend pod  → can only reach postgres on port 5432
  postgres pod → cannot initiate outbound connections at all
  Any other traffic → DROP
```

**Network Policies are enforced by the CNI plugin:**

```
Not all CNI plugins support NetworkPolicy!

Supports NetworkPolicy:
  Calico     — most feature-rich, supports global policies
  Cilium     — eBPF-based, high performance, Layer 7 support
  Weave      — simple setup
  Antrea     — VMware's CNI

Does NOT support NetworkPolicy:
  Flannel    — must pair with Calico for policy enforcement
  kubenet    — basic CNI (used in some cloud setups)

k3s default: Flannel (no NetworkPolicy support out of the box)
k3s with --cni=calico or --cni=cilium: full support

Note: in this sandbox, NetworkPolicies can be created but may not be
enforced depending on the k3s CNI configuration.
```

**A NetworkPolicy only applies to pods it selects:**

```
If no NetworkPolicy selects a pod → allow all (default behavior preserved)
If any NetworkPolicy selects a pod → that pod is isolated for that direction
  (ingress isolation if the policy has ingress rules,
   egress isolation if the policy has egress rules)

This means: adding a NetworkPolicy is additive — you whitelist.
There is no way to "deny" via NetworkPolicy; you only whitelist allowed traffic.
Everything else is denied once any policy selects the pod.
```

sections.title: NetworkPolicy anatomy: selectors and rules
sections.body:
**Basic structure:**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: my-policy
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:        # which pods this policy applies to
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:        # which direction(s) this policy controls
  - Ingress           # control incoming traffic to selected pods
  - Egress            # control outgoing traffic from selected pods
  ingress:
  - from:             # allow traffic FROM these sources
    - podSelector:    # from pods with this label in same namespace
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:            # on these ports
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
  egress:
  - to:               # allow traffic TO these destinations
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - port: 5432
```

**podSelector — which pods this policy applies to:**

```yaml
podSelector: {}              # empty = select ALL pods in namespace
podSelector:                 # specific pods by label
  matchLabels:
    app: api-server
podSelector:
  matchExpressions:          # more complex selection
  - key: tier
    operator: In
    values: ["frontend", "backend"]
```

**from/to selectors — filter traffic sources/destinations:**

```yaml
from:
# Option 1: pods in same namespace
- podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      role: monitoring

# Option 2: pods in a specific namespace
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring

# Option 3: specific namespace AND specific pods (AND logic)
- namespaceSelector:
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring
  podSelector:                  # same list item = AND
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus

# Option 4: either namespace OR pods (OR logic)
- namespaceSelector:            # separate list items = OR
    matchLabels:
      name: monitoring
- podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: prometheus

# Option 5: specific external IP ranges
- ipBlock:
    cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
    except:
    - 10.0.1.0/24             # exclude this subnet
```

**DNS egress — easy to forget:**

```yaml
# Without this, pods can't resolve hostnames!
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector:        # allow DNS queries to kube-dns
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
  ports:
  - port: 53
    protocol: UDP
  - port: 53
    protocol: TCP
```

sections.title: Common Network Policy patterns
sections.body:
**Pattern 1: Default deny all**

```yaml
# Apply to a namespace first, then whitelist specific traffic.
# The empty podSelector selects ALL pods; no ingress/egress = deny all.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}   # all pods
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  # No ingress or egress rules = deny everything
```

**Pattern 2: Allow only frontend → backend traffic**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: backend-ingress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
```

**Pattern 3: Namespace isolation (only allow traffic within namespace)**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: namespace-isolation
  namespace: staging
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: staging  # same namespace only
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: staging
  - to:  # also allow DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
```

**Pattern 4: Allow monitoring namespace to scrape metrics**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-prometheus-scrape
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}  # all pods in production
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
    ports:
    - port: 9090   # metrics endpoint
      protocol: TCP
```

**Pattern 5: Egress to specific external service only**

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-egress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api-server
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - podSelector:    # internal postgres
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - port: 5432
  - to:
    - ipBlock:         # external S3
        cidr: 52.216.0.0/14  # AWS S3 IP range (example)
    ports:
    - port: 443
  - to:  # DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
```

sections.title: Exercise: create and inspect Network Policies
sections.body:
Create network policies for a sample multi-tier application. Note: in this k3s sandbox (Flannel CNI), policies are created but enforcement depends on the CNI. We'll focus on writing and reading the policies correctly.

```bash
# ── 1. Label the namespaces (required for namespaceSelector) ──────────────
kubectl label namespace default kubernetes.io/metadata.name=default --overwrite
kubectl label namespace learning kubernetes.io/metadata.name=learning --overwrite
kubectl label namespace monitoring kubernetes.io/metadata.name=monitoring --overwrite

# ── 2. Create a deny-all policy for the learning namespace ────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
EOF

# ── 3. Create the three-tier app labels ──────────────────────────────────
# Label existing pods (we'll use the api-server deployment)
kubectl label deployment api-server -n learning tier=backend

# ── 4. Allow monitoring to scrape the backend ─────────────────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-monitoring-scrape
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      tier: backend
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: monitoring
    ports:
    - port: 9090
      protocol: TCP
    - port: 8080
      protocol: TCP
EOF

# ── 5. Allow DNS egress (required for any real workload) ──────────────────
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: learning
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
    - port: 53
      protocol: TCP
EOF

# ── 6. Inspect what we created ────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl get networkpolicies -n learning
kubectl describe networkpolicy default-deny-all -n learning
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-monitoring-scrape -n learning

# ── 7. Visualize the policy structure ────────────────────────────────────
python3 << 'PYEOF'
policies = [
    {"name": "default-deny-all",         "selects": "all pods", "ingress": "DENY ALL", "egress": "DENY ALL"},
    {"name": "allow-monitoring-scrape",   "selects": "tier=backend", "ingress": "FROM monitoring ns :9090,:8080", "egress": "-"},
    {"name": "allow-dns-egress",          "selects": "all pods", "ingress": "-", "egress": "TO kube-system :53/UDP"},
]

print(f"{'Policy':<30} {'Selects':<20} {'Ingress':<35} {'Egress'}")
print("-" * 100)
for p in policies:
    print(f"{p['name']:<30} {p['selects']:<20} {p['ingress']:<35} {p['egress']}")
PYEOF

# ── 8. Write a network policy for the default namespace ───────────────────
# Challenge: write a policy that allows:
#   - web-app pods to receive traffic from any pod in default namespace
#   - web-app pods to make outbound calls to the learning namespace on port 8080
kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: web-app-policy
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: default
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: learning
    ports:
    - port: 8080
  - to:  # DNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
    ports:
    - port: 53
      protocol: UDP
EOF

kubectl get networkpolicies -n default
kubectl get networkpolicies -n learning

# ── 9. Clean up ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete networkpolicy default-deny-all allow-monitoring-scrape allow-dns-egress -n learning
kubectl delete networkpolicy web-app-policy -n default 2>/dev/null || true
```

questions.q: A pod has a NetworkPolicy that only has policyTypes: [Ingress] with one ingress rule. What happens to its egress traffic?
options: All egress traffic is allowed (the policy only controls ingress)
Egress is denied unless there is also an Egress policy type
questions.explanation: NetworkPolicy only controls the direction(s) listed in policyTypes. If only Ingress is listed, egress traffic is unaffected by this policy (defaults to allow). You need to explicitly add Egress to policyTypes and egress rules to restrict outbound traffic.

questions.q: Two `from` entries in the same ingress rule — how are they evaluated?
questions.explanation: Separate items in the `from` array are OR conditions — traffic is allowed if it matches any one of them. To require AND (e.g., a specific namespace AND a specific pod label), both selectors must be in the SAME list item (as fields of the same object).

questions.q: You apply a default-deny-all NetworkPolicy to a namespace. Pods can no longer resolve DNS hostnames. Why?
options: DNS resolution requires UDP/TCP port 53 egress to kube-system, which is now blocked
NetworkPolicy doesn't affect DNS because DNS uses UDP
questions.explanation: DNS resolution sends queries to kube-dns (in kube-system namespace) on port 53/UDP (and sometimes TCP). A default-deny-all policy blocks all egress including DNS. You must add an explicit egress rule allowing port 53 UDP/TCP to the kube-system namespace.

sections.title: Challenge: design a zero-trust policy set for a three-tier app
sections.goal: Design (write as YAML) a complete set of NetworkPolicies for a three-tier application with pods labeled: tier=frontend, tier=backend, tier=database. Apply the principle of least privilege: frontend accepts traffic from anywhere on port 80; frontend can call backend on port 8080; backend can call database on port 5432; database cannot initiate any outbound connection; all tiers can resolve DNS.
hints: You need at least 4 policies: one default-deny, and then whitelist policies for each tier
Start with default-deny-all on the namespace, then add specific allow rules
Remember DNS egress (port 53 UDP to kube-system) for all tiers that need it
Use separate NetworkPolicy objects per tier for clarity rather than one complex policy
success_criteria: A default-deny-all policy exists for the namespace
frontend policy allows ingress from anywhere on port 80
frontend policy allows egress only to backend on port 8080 (plus DNS)
backend policy allows ingress only from frontend on port 8080
backend policy allows egress only to database on port 5432 (plus DNS)
database policy allows ingress only from backend on port 5432
database policy has no egress rules (denies all egress)
